ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Importantly, when simulating study-specific patient inclusion criteria, the model accurately reproduced stroke incidence in the general population (Figure 2A), post-stroke acute fatality (Figure 2B), non-fatal (Figure 2C) and fatal major bleeding (Figure 2D) incidences in the general population without OAC, as well as major bleeding in AF patients without (Figure 2E) or with OAC (Figure 2F).
table.formatted: Importantly, when simulating study-specific patient inclusion criteria, the model accurately reproduced stroke incidence in the general population (Figure <ref type="figure">2A</ref>), post-stroke acute fatality (Figure <ref type="figure">2B</ref>), non-fatal (Figure <ref type="figure">2C</ref>) and fatal major bleeding (Figure <ref type="figure">2D</ref>) incidences in the general population without OAC, as well as major bleeding in AF patients without (Figure <ref type="figure">2E</ref>) or with OAC (Figure <ref type="figure">2F</ref>).

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Importantly, when simulating study-specific patient inclusion criteria, the model accurately reproduced stroke incidence in the general population (Figure 2A), post-stroke acute fatality (Figure 2B), non-fatal (Figure 2C) and fatal major bleeding (Figure 2D) incidences in the general population without OAC, as well as major bleeding in AF patients without (Figure 2E) or with OAC (Figure 2F).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P=0.48", "P=0.47", "P=0.69", "P=0.52" ), Sentence = c("The predicted occurrence of the composite primary endpoint (stroke or all-cause mortality) at 5 years in patients was significantly higher in non-anticoagulated patients with AF and CHA2DS2-VASc=2 compared with those with either pill-in-pocket or continuous OAC (log-rank P<0.001, Figure 5A), while no significant difference was identified between pill-in-pocket and continuous OAC (HR: 1.04, 95%CI: 0.93-1.16, P=0.48, Table S8).", "In the baseline model, pill-in-pocket OAC did not lower major-bleeding incidence compared to continuous OAC (HR: 0.92, 95%CI: 0.74-1.15, P=0.47; Table S8).", "Of note, when assessing the individual components of the primary endpoint, the stroke risk was also significantly higher (HR: 1.50, 95%CI: 1.17-1.92, P=0.0014) while mortality was similar (HR:0.98, 95%CI: 0.87-1.10, P=0.69) with pill-in-pocket versus continuous OAC (Figure S4A-B and Table S8).", "However, in virtual populations with doubled baseline bleeding risk, the difference in stroke incidence between continuous and rhythm-guided OAC was diminished (HR: 0.92, 95% CI: 0.71-1.19, P=0.52) and major bleeding was significantly lower (HR: 0.81, 95% CI: 0.68-0.96, P=0.014) in pill-in-pocket strategy compared with continuous OAC (Figure S4C-D, Figure 5C-D and Table S9)." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.
